claims.claim: The blogger argues Hobb's first person in Assassin's Apprentice is less closely restricted to the child narrator than he expected, citing the phrase 'brackish iodine smell' on page 21 as a perception the six-year-old Fitz could not have had.
claims.quote: at that early point Fitz had no exposure to the world
claims.page: P.S. section at end of post
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: The blogger observes that Hobb renders dramatic events without melodrama: no character screams in pain or is shown in shock.
claims.quote: You don’t see melodrama, you don’t see the character screaming in pain
claims.page: body, paragraph on time jumps and Fitz's voice
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: The blogger characterises Fitz's narrating voice as understated rather than strongly defined, and credits that understatement with bringing the surrounding characters and places forward.
claims.quote: But I think Fitz voice is actually understated
claims.page: body, paragraph on time jumps
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: The blogger says the book is carried by prose rather than dialogue, with direct dialogue taking a secondary place.
claims.quote: it is prose first and foremost, with direct dialogue taking a backseat
claims.page: body, paragraph beginning 'This was the romantic view'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: The blogger complains that in the final chapters some actions of Assassin's Apprentice appear to carry no consequence, the aftermath being shrugged off by the characters.
claims.quote: some actions don’t seem to have any other consequence
claims.page: body, paragraph beginning 'Even here it’s not all “perfect.”'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.feature: other: pacing as the site of value
claims.claim: The blogger argues the slow pacing of Assassin's Apprentice is not a defect to be endured but where the book's value lies, and that the reading method it demands is staying in the present of the page rather than anticipating.
claims.quote: the slow pacing here isn’t a weak point to overcome
claims.page: body, paragraph after the quoted reader review
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: Reviewer Laura M. Hughes names the narrative voice, not plot or worldbuilding, as the novel's main strength.
claims.quote: the novel’s main strength is its narrative voice
claims.page: final body paragraph
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: Hughes contrasts Fitz with Rothfuss's Kvothe, arguing Fitz's self-deprecating narration reports the damning facts about his own actions rather than flattering him.
claims.quote: unlike Kvothe, Fitz is brutally honest
claims.page: final body paragraph
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: Novelist Natasha Pulley points out that Hobb declines the efficient move of simply naming the garden maid, and instead has two characters work out between them who she is.
claims.quote: which would have been the narratively efficient thing to do
claims.page: paragraph 3, 'There’s an unobtrusive moment'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: Pulley's close reading turns on one concrete noun: Fitz disputes the Fool's simile 'hair the colour of clean straw' because straw belongs to his stable upbringing and not to the Fool's.
claims.quote: What’s brilliant, though, is that he does it over straw
claims.page: paragraph 5, after the quoted dialogue
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: Pulley reads a passing quarrel over a minor descriptive detail as carrying, without statement, the class histories of both speakers.
claims.quote: It says volumes about both of them
claims.page: paragraph 5, last sentence
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.feature: other: small-scale detail beside large-scale spectacle
claims.claim: Pulley contrasts the trilogy's dragons, prophets and sweeping landscapes with what she calls its pin-sharp moments.
claims.quote: but it has these pin-sharp moments too
claims.page: final body paragraph
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: Novelist Steven Erikson says what he admired on first reading Assassin's Apprentice was the controlled point of view and the leisurely pace.
claims.quote: admired the controlled point of view, the leisurely pace
claims.page: paragraph 4, 'Started reading'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: Erikson reports that after the book's turning scene he reread the preceding pages line by line to find the hints Hobb had planted that he had missed.
claims.quote: deconstructing, line by line, to catch every subtle tell
claims.page: paragraph 6, 'Back to that scene'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: Erikson says he sets the opening chapters of Assassin's Apprentice as required reading on point of view in the writing workshops he teaches.
claims.quote: I cite the opening chapters of Assassin’s Apprentice as required reading
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'To this day in the workshops'

claims.claim: Erikson describes the child point of view in fantasy as a device that delivers knowledge to the reader piecemeal at the child's rate of comprehension, in an essay whose worked example is Hobb's Fitz.
claims.quote: Knowledge is fed piecemeal, at a child’s pace of comprehension
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'It’s no accident the child POV'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: Critic Adam Whitehead states the rule governing reliability in the Farseer narration: the further an event lies from Fitz's own perspective, the less reliable the account of it is.
claims.quote: the further things and events are from Fitz's perspective
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'Much of your enjoyment'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: Whitehead names a naturalistic manner of presenting the world, alongside characterisation, as Hobb's greatest strength.
claims.quote: her naturalistic way of presenting the world
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'Robin Hobb’s greatest strength'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: Whitehead names as Hobb's greatest weakness a tendency to meander, with characters sitting and talking about the plot at length.
claims.quote: a tendency to meander, to have characters sitting around talking
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'Robin Hobb’s greatest strength'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: Whitehead calls Hobb a superior prose writer and a gifted communicator of emotions and atmosphere.
claims.quote: Hobb is a superior prose writer and a gifted communicator
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'Hobb is a superior prose writer'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: Hobb, in her own transcribed words, says a farmer and a character from a sailing-ship background will choose different vocabulary for the same things, and gives her own house as the example, where the same rooms are galley, head and deck to her sailor husband and kitchen, bathroom and floor to her.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (transcript)
claims.quote: we have a galley, we have a head, we have a deck
claims.page: second half, 'Well, again, it’s knowing the character’s background'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: Hobb gives a test for per-speaker register: read a passage of dialogue and you should be able to tell who is speaking without the attribution tags.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (transcript)
claims.quote: you should be able to tell who is talking without
claims.page: second half, 'If you want to do a double check, read your dialogue'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: Hobb names sentence length as one of the carriers of per-speaker difference, saying some characters speak in longer sentences and some in shorter ones, using The Lord of the Rings as her example.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (transcript)
claims.quote: Some characters speak in longer sentences, some speak in shorter sentences
claims.page: second half, 'If you have two farmers'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: Hobb says she writes a great deal in first person because she regards it as the natural storytelling voice, likening it to a person recounting their day at home.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (transcript)
claims.quote: first person is the natural storytelling voice
claims.page: first half, 'I write… a tremendous amount of my work is first person'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: Hobb says what a first-person narrator notices on entering a room is determined by who he is, contrasting an assassin entering a room with three people in it against a child looking for a lost toy.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (transcript)
claims.quote: what he notices is going to be very different
claims.page: second half, 'If you’re writing from the first person'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: Hobb derives a character's personality from household economy, explaining a pennypinching character by a childhood family on a very tight budget in which every choice was consequential.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (transcript)
claims.quote: Charlotte grew up in a family with a very tight budget
claims.page: first half, 'Why is she so pennypinching?'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: Hobb says that for her the character has to be generated by the world, and that she could not believably insert a twenty-first century person into a fantasy.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (transcript)
claims.quote: the character has to be generated by the world
claims.page: first half, answer to the opening question
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.feature: other: reaction to a minor character as characterisation
claims.claim: Hobb offers an inn scene as a characterisation test: a late serving boy, and whether the viewpoint character fails to notice, is annoyed at someone else's shouting, is embarrassed, or quietly tips the boy.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (transcript)
claims.quote: whether you quietly tip the kid
claims.page: second half, 'How a character treats a secondary character'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: The essayist argues Hobb's method is to place the reader inside Fitz's perspective and leave them there, supplying no outside witness to frame him.
claims.source: The Huntress And The Wolf, Substack, 15 February 2026
claims.quote: Hobb places you inside Fitz’s perspective and leaves you there
claims.page: opening section, 'Robin Hobb’s great trick'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: The essayist argues that Fitz's competence is legible only by inference because he almost never narrates his own power, reporting instead his doubts, failures, grief and shame.
claims.source: The Huntress And The Wolf, Substack, 15 February 2026
claims.quote: he almost never narrates his own power
claims.page: section 'A Wild Soul'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: The essayist shows Hobb rendering a character's training as an inventory of ordinary objects in a room, listing medicinal unguents on the mantel, two pens at the ready and a Stones puzzle on the table.
claims.source: The Huntress And The Wolf, Substack, 15 February 2026
claims.quote: the medicinal unguents on the mantel, the two pens
claims.page: section 'A Master of His Craft'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: The essayist argues that Fitz-as-chronicler records what official chroniclers could not, and that history in Hobb is made in bedrooms, kitchens, stables and sickrooms as well as in councils and battles.
claims.source: The Huntress And The Wolf, Substack, 15 February 2026
claims.quote: history is not made only in councils and battles
claims.page: section 'A Writer, Historian, and Chronicler of His Age'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: The essayist warns that the intimacy of Fitz's prose should not be mistaken for simplicity, crediting it with clear rendering of character, politics, landscape, memory and moral conflict.
claims.source: The Huntress And The Wolf, Substack, 15 February 2026
claims.quote: intimacy should not be mistaken for simplicity
claims.page: section 'A Writer, Historian, and Chronicler of His Age'
claims.routeHint: raw curl with browser user agent

claims.claim: The essayist says Hobb hides her protagonist's magnificence in plain sight, leaving it to the reader whether to see past his harsh self-assessment.
claims.source: The Huntress And The Wolf, Substack, 15 February 2026
claims.quote: She hides his magnificence in plain sight
